prompt: Which economist co-wrote The Calculus of Consent (1962) with Gordon Tullock, launching modern public choice theory?
explanation: Buchanan and Tullock's The Calculus of Consent founded the modern field, and Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel. Downs is known for rational ignorance, Arrow for his impossibility theorem and North for institutional economics.

prompt: Anthony Downs argued that because one vote almost never decides an election, it is rational for voters to stay largely uninformed about policy. This is called rational _________.
explanation: Rational ignorance follows from comparing the real cost of becoming informed with the tiny expected benefit, since one voter's influence is microscopic. It reflects incentives, not a lack of intelligence.

prompt: Why do policies such as sugar subsidies persist even when their net welfare effect is negative?
options: Benefits are concentrated on a few producers while costs are spread thinly across many consumers
Consumers strongly support higher sugar prices
Economists agree the subsidies raise total welfare
The costs fall mainly on the producers who lobby for them
correctAnswer: Benefits are concentrated on a few producers while costs are spread thinly across many consumers
explanation: Concentrated beneficiaries have strong incentives to lobby, while each consumer loses too little to notice or organize. This political asymmetry lets such policies pass and persist.

prompt: Public choice theory models politicians and bureaucrats as benevolent stewards of the public good.
explanation: The radical move of public choice is to treat politicians, voters, bureaucrats and lobbyists as self-interested agents, just like market participants. Critics argue this is too cynical, but it is the framework's core assumption.

prompt: Which institution is an example of a rule that limits political short-termism?
explanation: Vote-maximizing politicians favor visible short-term gains with deferred costs. Independent central banks, balanced-budget rules and judicial review constrain that tendency, at the price of some democratic flexibility.

prompt: Three voters rank candidates as A > B > C, B > C > A and C > A > B. What do pairwise majority votes produce?
options: A cycle: A beats B, B beats C and C beats A
Every head-to-head contest is a tie
B wins as the compromise candidate
correctAnswer: A cycle: A beats B, B beats C and C beats A
explanation: Each head-to-head contest is won 2-1, but the winners form a loop, so there is no consistent majority winner. This is the Condorcet paradox: rational individual preferences can produce intransitive collective preferences.

prompt: Which of these are conditions in Arrow's impossibility theorem? (Select all that apply.)
correctAnswer: Universal domain | Pareto | Independence of irrelevant alternatives | Non-dictatorship
explanation: Arrow's conditions are universal domain, Pareto, independence of irrelevant alternatives, non-dictatorship and transitive social preferences. Single-peaked preferences are a restriction that escapes the theorem, and strategy-proofness belongs to the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem.

prompt: Match each voting rule to how it works:

pairs.right: The candidate with the most first-place votes wins
Voters approve every acceptable candidate and the most-approved wins
Candidates with the fewest first-place votes are eliminated and their votes redistributed

explanation: Each rule aggregates the same preferences differently and can produce different winners. Plurality uses only first choices, Borda scores full rankings, approval asks a yes/no question per candidate, and instant runoff eliminates candidates in rounds.

prompt: Arrow's impossibility theorem applies even when there are only two alternatives.
explanation: The theorem requires three or more alternatives. With just two options, simple majority rule satisfies all of Arrow's conditions.

prompt: Ranked-choice (instant runoff) voting can violate which property, so that ranking a candidate higher can paradoxically hurt them?
explanation: Under instant runoff, extra support for a candidate can change the elimination order and cause them to lose. That is a monotonicity failure, which is different from the spoiler problem (an IIA failure) that plagues plurality.

prompt: What condition does Black's median voter theorem require for majority rule to select the median voter's preferred outcome?
options: Single-peaked preferences along a single dimension
correctAnswer: Single-peaked preferences along a single dimension
explanation: When each voter's preferences peak at one point on a single dimension and fall away on either side, the median voter's ideal beats every alternative in pairwise majority votes. With multiple dimensions there may be no clear median.

prompt: In Hotelling's beach model, two ice cream vendors competing for customers both end up at the _________ of the beach.
explanation: Each vendor gains by moving toward the other, so both converge on the center and split the customers. The political analog is two parties converging on the median voter's position.

prompt: Which of these help explain why real parties often do not converge on the median voter? (Select all that apply.)
options: Primary elections dominated by partisan voters
Mobilizing the base can matter more than persuading swing voters
Big donors hold positions away from the median
Voters have single-peaked preferences on one dimension
Competition is strictly between two parties
correctAnswer: Preferences span multiple dimensions | Primary elections dominated by partisan voters | Mobilizing the base can matter more than persuading swing voters | Big donors hold positions away from the median
acceptableAnswers: Primary elections dominated by partisan voters
Mobilizing the base can matter more than persuading swing voters
Big donors hold positions away from the median
explanation: Multidimensional preferences, primaries, turnout effects and donor influence all pull candidates away from the center. Single-peaked preferences on one dimension and two-party competition are the theorem's own assumptions, which favor convergence.

prompt: Under the median voter theorem's assumptions, the median voter's preferred policy beats every alternative in a pairwise majority vote.
explanation: With single-peaked preferences on one dimension, any alternative is opposed by the median voter plus everyone on the median's side of it, which is a majority. So the median voter is decisive.

prompt: In a proportional-representation system, which party often gains power beyond its vote share?
options: A pivotal party whose support is needed to form a majority coalition
The largest party, which always governs alone
Whichever party wins the most single-member districts
The party closest to the median voter, by law
correctAnswer: A pivotal party whose support is needed to form a majority coalition
explanation: Under proportional representation, coalitions form after the election, and a party whose votes are needed for a majority can extract concessions. That is why small parties can wield outsized influence.

prompt: Whose 1967 paper argued that the resources spent to obtain a monopoly are an extra social cost beyond the deadweight loss triangle?
explanation: Tullock noticed that lobbying, legal fees and campaigns to win monopoly rights consume real resources. This rent-seeking cost comes on top of the familiar deadweight loss.

prompt: Tullock's full-dissipation result implies that the social cost of a monopoly can be as large as the whole monopoly profit plus the deadweight loss.
explanation: If competing rent-seekers collectively spend up to the full value of the rent, all of the monopoly profit is burned in the contest. Adding the deadweight loss gives the total social cost. The result is extreme but shows why the triangle alone understates the damage.

prompt: From a social perspective, why is rent seeking considered wasteful?
options: It uses up resources to transfer existing wealth rather than create new output
It always reduces the rent-seeker's own profits
It is illegal in most advanced economies
correctAnswer: It uses up resources to transfer existing wealth rather than create new output
explanation: A lobbyist's effort moves wealth from one group to another while burning resources in the process. Rent seeking is usually legal and privately profitable, which is exactly why it persists.

prompt: Sort each activity by whether it is rent seeking or productive activity:
explanation: Rent seeking spends resources to capture or defend artificial rents such as quotas, loopholes or licensing fees. Productive activity creates new output or lowers costs, adding to the total rather than redistributing it.

prompt: What did Murphy, Shleifer and Vishny (1991) argue about economies with large available rents?
options: Talented people are drawn into rent seeking instead of production, slowing growth
Rents are quickly competed away and have no effect on growth
Rent seeking speeds up innovation by rewarding lobbyists
Large rents make institutions stronger over time
correctAnswer: Talented people are drawn into rent seeking instead of production, slowing growth
explanation: When rent seeking pays better than entrepreneurship, the most talented people pursue it and the economy can get stuck in a low equilibrium. Reducing rents reorients talent toward production.

prompt: How did Douglass North define institutions?
options: The rules of the game in a society
The government agencies that run the economy
The physical infrastructure of a country
correctAnswer: The rules of the game in a society
explanation: North defined institutions as the formal and informal rules that structure incentives, from laws and constitutions to norms and conventions. They are rules, not organizations or physical assets.

prompt: Match each thinker to the idea associated with them:

pairs.right: Institutions as the rules of the game
Transaction costs explain why firms exist

explanation: North framed institutions as rules structuring incentives, and Coase explained firms and markets through transaction costs. De Soto showed how homes without legal title cannot serve as collateral, and Acemoglu and Robinson stress that reform needs changing the coalitions that benefit from bad institutions.

prompt: Coase argued that externalities are always resolved efficiently through private bargaining, even when transaction costs are high.
explanation: Coase's point was that bargaining can resolve externalities only if transaction costs are zero. Real bargaining costs are positive and often prohibitive, which is exactly why property rights and legal rules matter.

prompt: Hernando de Soto described the wealth tied up in homes that lack legal title, and so cannot serve as collateral, as _________ capital.
explanation: Without formal title, property cannot be reliably sold or used to secure loans. De Soto argued that formalizing property rights would unlock this dead capital.

prompt: A peasant 'owns' land but is forbidden to sell it. Which dimension of property rights is missing?
explanation: Property rights have three dimensions: ownership clarity, use rights and transfer rights. Being unable to sell, lease or bequeath the land is a lack of transfer rights.
